in_text_mentions: by occupational exposure to white phosphorus which was called “phossy jaw” [44, 45]. ONJ has also seen in osteopetrosis, a rare inherited disease with impairment of bone resorption and remodeling [46]. More recently, ONJ is defined as a complication of head and neck radiotherapy [47]. The definition of ONJ is nonhealing exposed jawbone for more than 8 weeks in patients receiving BPs and without any local radiation therapy. Clinically, the disease presents as exposed alveolar bone that becomes evident following a surgical procedure such as tooth removal or periodontal therapy [48, 49] Figure 2.

Unfortunately, 4 months after the extraction, the site was painful with exposed bone and poor healing consistent with medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. Normal bone healing after a dental extraction would have shown mucosal coverage within a month

in_text_mentions: As other types of osteonecrosis determined by different etiologies, BRONJ is characterized by the presence of osteocyte-depleted bone lacunae. Our diagnostic experience suggests that this avascular necrosis is characterized by lacunae osteocyte depletion which is more obvious in the deeper layers of the bone while the lacunae located towards the surface of the bone lamellae will lose the osteocytes at a later stage (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: , continuing to challenge clinical decision-making in dental practice. Several studies have suggested that patients undergoing antiresorptive therapy may have a relatively low risk of developing osteonecrosis of the jaws (ONJ) following dental implant placement when compared to non-medicated individuals [7]. However, this risk is influenced by multiple factors, including the type of drug, dosage, duration of therapy and the patient’s individual risk profile [8]. Conversely, numerous case reports [9] have documented the occurrence of MRONJ associated with implant-related procedures. (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (1A, 1B-clinical, 1B-radiograph, 1C-intraoral, 1C-extraoral, 1C-radiograph). 1A: Intraoral clinical photo described as stage 1 MRONJ with small asymptomatic exposed necrotic bone in breast cancer patient on zoledronic acid. 1B-clinical: Intraoral clinical photo of denosumab patient with non-healing extraction site and exposed alveolar bone with pain not responding to antibiotics. 1B-radiograph: Periapical radiograph described as showing non-healing alveolus in same MRONJ patient with exposed bone. 1C-intraoral: Intraoral clinical photo of multiple myeloma patient with Stage 3 MRONJ described with swelling, infected exposed bone with pus drainage. 1C-extraoral: Extraoral clinical photo showing draining fistula in left submandibular area in Stage 3 MRONJ patient. 1C-radiograph: Panoramic-type radiograph described with extensive bone destruction at risk for pathological fracture in Stage 3 MRONJ.

panels.figure_caption: Shows clinical and radiographical images of different stages of MRONJ. (A): stage 1 showing a patient with breast cancer taking zoledronic acid with a small asymptomatic area of exposed necrotic bone that was affecting the use of a removable prosthodontic appliance. (B): shows a patient taking denosumab who had a recent dental extraction. The site was not healing, and exposed alveolar bone could be seen. The patient was in pain and did not respond to antibiotics. The radiographical image shows the non-healing alveolus. (C): shows a patient with multiple myeloma with Stage 3 MRONJ. The patient was in pain and presented to the clinic with swelling of the alveolar mucosa and several areas of infected and exposed bone with pus drainage. The patient complained of paresthesia in the area and had a strong mal odor. One can observe an extraoral fistula on the left submandibular area. The radiograph shows the extensive area of bone destruction, placing the patient at risk for a pathological fracture. Note that the fixed prosthodontic appliance was removed, revealing the exposed bone seen in this figure.
in_text_mentions: In addition to a precise definition and diagnosis, one should stage the complication before management is proposed (Figure 1). Staging of MRONJ is of importance in the decision-making process on how to manage each of the patients. Periosteal reaction was observed either prior to or concurrently with the appearance of MRONJ demarcation line (Fig. 3). Periosteal reaction was observed as part of the healing process (Fig. 3). Previous studies have described periosteal reaction as a risk factor for treatment failure due to bacterial infection [23, 24]. None of the patients with periosteal reaction were cured by conservative treatment, indicating that surgical intervention may be the only effective option [14]. in_text_mentions: The patients who came with MRONJ in the surgery clinic were investigated by computer tomograph scanning. For most of them, a CT scan was performed both to clarify the diagnosis and assess the extent of the bone lesion but also to establish the surgical treatment plan. in_text_mentions: However, after 2 years of follow-up, the patient presented with a main complaint of nonhealing sockets following multiple tooth extractions (Fig. 3A and B). The clinical history and radiographic features were consistent with the diagnosis of MRONJ as the patient had no clinical evidence of necrotic bone but presented with aching bone pain in the jaw. The axial CBCT confirmed the presence of sequestra formation and a pathological fracture, categorizing the patient as stage 3.Fig. 3Case 3: (A) The panoramic radiograph revealed a moth-eaten appearance associated with the extraction sockets of the

Histopathologic assessment (Fig. 3C) of both the mandibular and maxillary bone biopsies revealed the presence of nonvital bone with an irregular surface outline due to resorption. Abundant basophilic bacteria colonized the bone surface, with evidence of acute inflammation. No features concerning plasma cell neoplasm were observed. The patient subsequently died due to medical complications.

in_text_mentions: A 61‐year‐old woman (T.R.) presented to our clinic with severe pain and noticeable swelling in the right posterior maxilla. Clinical examination revealed a persistent intraoral fistula with purulent discharge and exposed necrotic bone, easily identified upon probing. Radiographic evaluation via cone‐beam CT (CBCT) demonstrated a large osteolytic lesion with clear signs of sequestration and complete maxillary sinus opacification consistent with MRONJ stage 3 (Figure 7).

panels.figure_caption: Periosteal reaction. (A) Attached-type, (B) gap-type, and (C) irregular-type.
in_text_mentions: e mandibular canal was included in the mandibular cases, and “none” if no bone resorption was observed except for the remaining extraction socket (Figure 1). According to the classification of Soutome et al., periosteal reactions were classified as “none,” “attached-type,” “gap-type,” and “irregular-type” (Figure 2) [16,18]. Furthermore, we defined mixed-type osteosclerosis [20] as the presence of multiple small radiolucent areas within marked osteosclerosis (Figure 3). Treatment outcome was defined as “healing” if all symptoms, including bone exposure, disappeared and “non-healing” otherwise.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Caption attributes right mandibular pathological fracture to MRONJ in disease-focused MRONJ article; cortical destruction fits cortical erosion vocabulary. B: Caption explicitly lists MRONJ sclerosis, lytic lesion and subperiosteal reaction in mandible. C: Caption attributes lysis, sclerosis and sequestration to MRONJ. D: MRONJ sequestration and sclerosis identified on panoramic CBCT reconstruction. E: Upper panoramic and lower axial CBCT show MRONJ maxillary sequestration and sclerosis. F: Caption attributes extensive mandibular lysis to MRONJ on panoramic CBCT reconstruction. G: MDCT shows MRONJ lysis and sclerosis with lamina dura thickening.
panels.attribution_text: Ghanaiem et al. Radiographic Analysis of MRONJ in Osteoporotic and Oncologic Patients on Bisphosphonates or Denosumab.. Oral diseases 2026. doi:10.1111/odi.70030. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Representative radiographic features of MRONJ. (A) Right mandibular pathological fracture (blue arrow); left: Three‐dimensional MDCT reconstruction, right: Panoramic radiograph. (B) Right mandibular sclerosis (blue arrow), lytic lesion (red arrow), and subperiosteal reaction (green arrow); upper: Panoramic CBCT reconstruction, lower: Axial CBCT sections. (C) Extensive right mandibular lysis (red arrow), sclerosis (blue arrow), and sequestration (yellow arrow); upper: Panoramic CBCT reconstruction, lower: Axial CBCT sections. (D) Left mandibular sequestration (yellow arrow), sclerosis (blue arrow), and unhealed extraction sites (black arrows); panoramic CBCT reconstruction. (E) Left maxillary sequestration (yellow arrow), sclerosis (red arrow), and maxillary sinus opacification (white arrow); upper: Panoramic CBCT reconstruction, lower: Axial CBCT sections. (F) Extensive right mandibular lysis (red arrow); panoramic CBCT reconstruction. (G) Extensive left mandibular lysis (red arrow), sclerosis (blue arrow) and thickening of the lamina dura (white arrow heads); MDCT.
in_text_mentions: Some of the most common radiographic features of MRONJ include lytic change, sclerosis, periosteal bone formation, sequestration, thickening of the lamina dura, and destruction of the periodontal ligament (Figure 1) (Shin et al. 2024).

In MRONJ, sclerosis is seen as increased bone density due to suppressed bone turnover from antiresorptive medications and chronic inflammation, and lysis involves bone destruction resulting from progressive necrosis and secondary infection (Obermeier et al. 2024) (Zhang et al. 2016). In addition, as a response to this abnormal stimulus, a periosteal reaction may also be seen as a nonspecific radiologic finding that demonstrates new bone formation from the abnormal stimuli (Soutome et al. 2021) (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is a pre-treatment CT example of MRONJ with caption 'separation of the sequestrum' and in-text definition of radiolucent area between necrotic bone and surrounding bone. Shows sequestrum directly. B: Panel B is a pre-treatment CT in MRONJ article with caption 'osteolysis above the mandibular canal'. No exact vocabulary key for CT osteolysis exists, so manifestation recorded as proposed finding; panel is real patient CT showing ONJ manifestation. C: Panel C is a pre-treatment CT in MRONJ article with caption 'osteolysis including the mandibular canal'. No exact vocabulary key for CT osteolysis exists, so manifestation recorded as proposed finding; panel is real patient CT showing ONJ manifestation. D: Panel D is a pre-treatment CT example of MRONJ with caption 'periosteal reaction', matching cortical erosion with periosteal reaction vocabulary term.

in_text_mentions: In this study, we focused on the trabecular changes in cancellous bone and classified the MRONJ lesions into two types, including osteosclerotic and osteolytic lesions (Fig. 1A, B; Fig. 2A, B). We defined osteosclerotic lesions as the increased alveolar bone density without any other trabecular changes. Once osteolysis occurs, the radiographic type of MRONJ lesions was classified as osteolytic lesions. The osteosclerotic lesion only presented as sclerosis in CT imaging, while the osteolytic lesion could involve many CT imaging features, such as osteolysis, sequestrum and sclerosis. The defined

plate_findings.evidence: (A) Intraoral presentation. Intraoral examination revealed an area of exposed necrotic bone located along the external oblique ridge of the right mandible
(B) Extraoral presentation of the cutaneous fistula on the lower right side of the mandible / A fistulous tract with purulent exudate was also observed

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Intraoral clinical photo shows exposed necrotic jaw bone, described in-text as exposed necrotic bone along external oblique ridge, hallmark of MRONJ in article about Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw. B: Extraoral clinical photo shows cutaneous fistula / draining sinus on right mandible, explicitly captioned as cutaneous fistula in MRONJ case. C: Extraoral clinical photo shows same cutaneous fistula with visible purulent discharge upon pressure, supporting draining fistula from necrotic jaw in MRONJ.

panels.figure_caption: (A) Intraoral presentation. (B) Extraoral presentation of the cutaneous fistula on the lower right side of the mandible. (C) Purulent discharge upon pressure on the right cheek
in_text_mentions: region exhibiting purulent discharge. The patient also reported paraesthesia involving the right lower lip and chin. Intraoral examination revealed an area of exposed necrotic bone located along the external oblique ridge of the right mandible, rather than the alveolar crest (Figure 1A). The surrounding mucosa showed signs of inflammation. A whitish material adherent to the exposed bone was identified and later determined to be glass ionomer cement (GIC) previously placed by a dentist in an attempt to seal the fistula. A fistulous tract with purulent exudate was also observed (Figures 1B, 1C).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: HE of surgically removed MRONJ mandible specimen showing necrotic bone with absent osteoblasts, matching avascular necrotic bone histology; article title confirms medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. in_text_mentions: T) imaging revealed extensive pathological changes involving the right mandibular body, characterized by a mixed osteolytic-sclerotic pattern with marked disruption of the normal bone architecture. Sagittal sections confirmed the presence of a pathological fracture, with irregular and poorly defined bone margins, as well as areas suggestive of sequestrum formation. The radiopaque GIC mass was again visualized within the fracture gap. Additionally, a hypodense tract extending inferiorly toward the cutaneous surface was identified, consistent with the course of the cutaneous fistula (Figure 3A).

Axial sections demonstrated significant osteolysis, with loss of normal trabecular organization and clear discontinuity of both the buccal and lingual cortical plates. A complete fracture line was identified, separating the mandibular body into two distinct segments. A well-defined hyperdense radiopaque mass, corresponding to the previously placed GIC, was observed interposed between the fractured segments (Figure 3B).

in_text_mentions: Approximately 12 months later, she presented with mild discomfort in the left posterior mandible. Intraoral examination revealed a small mucosal fistula with purulent discharge and surrounding inflammation (Figure 2A).

At the 12‐month follow‐up presentation, panoramic radiography showed focal osteolysis with irregular margins in the left mandibular molar region (Figure 2B). Computed tomography demonstrated osteolytic change in the lingual alveolar bone superior to the mandibular canal (Figure 2C).

s that coincided with the subsequent development of MRONJ. Furthermore, while PET/CT demonstrated distinct metabolic activity (SUVmax: 5.1), concurrent panoramic radiography and CT were completely unremarkable, lacking any signs of osteosclerosis or osteolysis [3, 4]. The longitudinal progression from this isolated metabolic abnormality (Figure 1) to the overt clinical and radiological bone destruction 12 months later (Figure 2) explicitly links our imaging findings to our clinical hypothesis: functional imaging can capture the early, subclinical phase of MRONJ before anatomical changes occur.
